metaTitle: Bugs That Look Like Cockroaches: 8 to Rule Out
metaDescription: Ground beetles, June bugs, earwigs, crickets and wood roaches get mistaken for cockroaches. See the size, antenna and body clues that tell them apart.
h1: Bugs That Look Like Cockroaches: How to Tell Each One Apart
dek: Ground beetles, June bugs, wood roaches, earwigs and crickets all get mistaken for pest cockroaches. Here are the size, antenna and body clues that separate them, with the sources behind each one.
excerpt: Ground beetles, June bugs, earwigs, crickets and wood roaches are often mistaken for cockroaches. The size, antenna and body clues that tell them apart.

quickAnswer.lead: **Ground beetles, June bugs, earwigs and crickets can all pass for cockroaches, and one test sorts them: a cockroach has a flat body, a plate that hides its head from above and long, thin antennae.** [Texas A&M AgriLife Extension](https://mytexas.ag.tamu.edu/publications/cockroach-biology-and-management/) describes that body plan. Wood cockroaches and palmetto bugs are real cockroaches, but a wood cockroach that gets indoors dies within days without breeding.
bullets: Texas A&M gives adult pest cockroach lengths from 1/2 to 5/8 inch for the German cockroach up to 1 1/2 to 2 inches for the American cockroach.
Adult ground beetles are mostly 1/4 to 3/4 inch, with hard wing covers that meet in a straight line down the back, and many fly to lights at night.
May beetles, also called June bugs, are 1/2 to 1 inch long and stout, usually brown, rusty or black, with clubbed antennae, and the Missouri Department of Conservation says they cannot hurt people.
Male wood cockroaches reach 1 inch and sometimes fly to lights, but Penn State Extension says they die within a few days indoors and do not reproduce there.
The adult European earwig is about 3/4 inch long and reddish brown, with forceps-like pincers at the tail end, and UC IPM says earwigs are not harmful to people.
Palmetto bug is a nickname, not a species: Texas A&M lists it as another name for the American cockroach.

body.text: How do you tell a cockroach from a look-alike?

Look for three features together: a flat body, a plate that hides the head from above, and long, thin antennae. That is the test to apply to the usual look-alikes: ground beetles, May beetles (June bugs), earwigs, crickets and outdoor wood cockroaches. [Texas A&M AgriLife Extension's guide to cockroach biology and management](https://mytexas.ag.tamu.edu/publications/cockroach-biology-and-management/) describes cockroaches as flattened insects whose heads are concealed from above by a plate called the pronotum, with long, thin antennae and elongated, spiny legs on which they move surprisingly fast.

No single feature settles it, because many harmless insects are brown and active at night, so use the checks below together. The species that actually infest US homes are laid out in [the complete guide to cockroaches](/learn/cockroaches).

Size is the next filter. The same Texas A&M guide gives adult lengths of 1/2 to 5/8 inch for the German cockroach, about 1 1/4 inches for the Oriental cockroach, 1 1/4 to 1 1/2 inches for the smokybrown cockroach and 1 1/2 to 2 inches for the American cockroach. None of those four is listed below 1/2 inch as an adult, so an insect well under that size is unlikely to be a full-grown example of any of them. It may be a young cockroach or a different insect, and [a separate guide shows what baby cockroaches look like](/blog/what-do-baby-cockroaches-look-like) species by species.
Then run these checks in order. Each of the first four points to a specific look-alike; long, thin antennae on their own do not confirm a cockroach.

items: **Antennae.** Antennae that end in a club point to a May beetle, according to the [Missouri Department of Conservation's May beetle page](https://mdc.mo.gov/discover-nature/field-guide/may-beetles-june-bugs). Long, thin antennae fit the cockroach Texas A&M describes, but keep checking.

**Back.** Shell-like wing covers that meet in a straight line over the abdomen mark a beetle, including the ground beetles on the [Missouri Department of Conservation's ground beetle page](https://mdc.mo.gov/discover-nature/field-guide/ground-beetles-carabids).
**Tail end.** A pair of prominent, forceps-like appendages means an earwig, as [UC IPM's earwig page](https://ipm.ucanr.edu/home-and-landscape/earwigs/) explains.

**Hind legs.** Hind legs adapted for jumping, together with chirping at night, mean a cricket, per the [Missouri Department of Conservation's field cricket page](https://mdc.mo.gov/discover-nature/field-guide/field-crickets).

**Where and when.** An insect found on firewood or beside a porch light may be an outdoor species such as a wood cockroach, which [Penn State Extension](https://extension.psu.edu/wood-cockroaches) says can arrive on firewood or after being drawn to porch lights.

body.text: Which bugs get mistaken for cockroaches?

Ground beetles, May beetles (June bugs), earwigs and crickets are the usual look-alikes, along with two true cockroaches that cause confusion: the outdoor wood cockroach and the palmetto bug. The table sets each one beside the trait that separates it from a pest cockroach. Giant water bugs and bed bugs are covered after the table.

body.caption: Sizes and traits come from Texas A&M AgriLife Extension, Penn State Extension, the Missouri Department of Conservation and the University of California Statewide IPM Program. Each source is linked in the sections below.

body.text: Is a wood cockroach the same as the roaches that infest homes?

No. A wood cockroach is a true cockroach that lives outdoors and does not reproduce indoors. [Penn State Extension's wood cockroach page](https://extension.psu.edu/wood-cockroaches) describes wood cockroaches as native *Parcoblatta* species, twelve of which occur in North America, and says they live in damp places with plenty of decaying organic matter, such as leaf litter, fallen logs, loose bark, wood piles and under stones. One that gets inside dies within a few days from dehydration and does not feed or reproduce there.

Males grow up to 1 inch (25 mm) long and have long wings that cover the abdomen. Females are up to 3/4 inch (19 mm) long with short wings that do not work. Colors run from light brown to nearly black, and some species have cream-colored stripes. Penn State says males can fly and are sometimes drawn to lights at night in rural areas. It contrasts wood cockroaches with the American cockroach, which is much larger at up to 2 inches and reddish brown, and with the Oriental cockroach, which is dark brown to nearly black.

Penn State lists the ways they get in: through cracks in a foundation or around windows and doors, on firewood, or after being attracted to porch lights. Its advice is to keep them out, and it says pesticides are not necessary or recommended. A separate guide explains [which cockroaches fly and which only glide](/blog/can-cockroaches-fly), and another covers [each route cockroaches use to get indoors](/blog/where-do-cockroaches-come-from).
Is a palmetto bug a different insect from a cockroach?

No. Palmetto bug is a nickname, and Texas A&M AgriLife Extension lists it, along with waterbug, as another name for the American cockroach. That species is the largest cockroach in Texas at 1 1/2 to 2 inches long, reddish brown, with tan to light yellow bands outlining the plate behind its head. Both males and females can fly.

Texas A&M adds that American, Oriental and smokybrown cockroaches live mostly outdoors but may move indoors in search of food or water. By that usage, a palmetto bug in the house is a pest cockroach that has come inside, not a harmless look-alike. The nickname is also applied to other large cockroaches, so go by the insect's features, not its name. The German cockroach is a different case: Texas A&M says German cockroaches spend their lives indoors.
Are ground beetles and June bugs cockroaches?

No. Both are beetles, which the Missouri Department of Conservation places in the order Coleoptera, while Penn State Extension places cockroaches in the order Blattodea. The shell-like wing covers that meet in a straight line down a beetle's back are the clearest sign.
How do you recognize a ground beetle?

A ground beetle has shell-like wing covers, called elytra, that meet in a straight line over the abdomen, as on other beetles, according to the [Missouri Department of Conservation's ground beetle page](https://mdc.mo.gov/discover-nature/field-guide/ground-beetles-carabids). Most are black or brown, often shiny, and many have lengthwise grooves on the wing covers. Their legs are long and slender and most are fast runners, a trait they share with cockroaches. The department puts the length of most species at 1/4 to 3/4 inch, though some North American species reach 2 inches.

Many ground beetles are nocturnal, hide in dark places by day and can fly to lights at night. The department describes them as predators that seek dark places under debris, where overturning a rock or log sends a few rushing away. Many of them eat cutworms and other caterpillars and grubs that injure crops, and some species emit or spray a foul or irritating chemical in defense.
How do you recognize a May beetle or June bug?

A May beetle, also called a June bug, is a stout, oval beetle, usually brown, rusty or black, with no spots or stripes and rather hairy underneath. Those details come from the [Missouri Department of Conservation's May beetle page](https://mdc.mo.gov/discover-nature/field-guide/may-beetles-june-bugs), which gives adult length as 1/2 to 1 inch and notes clubbed antennae. A cockroach's antennae, by contrast, are long and thin.

Adults are nocturnal and come to lights. The department calls them clumsy: they walk and fly awkwardly, and around porch lights on late-spring evenings they crash-land and lie on their backs waving their legs. They chew plant leaves and, the department says, cannot hurt people. Their whitish, C-shaped grubs live underground for one to four years, depending on the species, and can damage lawns and crops when numerous.

body.text: Do earwigs and crickets look like cockroaches?

Both can at a glance, and each has one giveaway: the pincers at an earwig's tail end and the jumping hind legs on a cricket. [UC IPM's earwig page](https://ipm.ucanr.edu/home-and-landscape/earwigs/), which names the European earwig (*Forficula auricularia*) as the most common species in California gardens, describes the adult as about 3/4 inch long and reddish brown and says it is readily identified by a pair of prominent appendages at the tail end that resemble forceps. The pincers may look ferocious, but the page states that earwigs are not harmful to people and generally do not attack humans, although they can bite if trapped in clothing or sat upon.

Earwigs feed most actively at night and hide by day in dark, cool, moist places such as under boards, soil clods or dense vines and weeds. UC IPM says they may come indoors when conditions outside are too dry, too hot or too cold, and it calls large accumulations of earwigs annoying but not a health hazard. If you were bitten and are trying to work out by what, a separate guide covers [what is documented about cockroaches biting people](/blog/do-cockroaches-bite).

Crickets are the other common indoor confusion. Field and house crickets have large heads and hind legs adapted for jumping, with stout spines, according to the [Missouri Department of Conservation's field cricket page](https://mdc.mo.gov/discover-nature/field-guide/field-crickets). Field crickets (genus *Gryllus*) are usually shiny black. The house cricket (*Acheta domesticus*) is light brown or tannish, with three dark crossbands on a tan head. Length is usually 1/2 to 1 inch.

Males chirp by rubbing their wings together, and crickets are nocturnal. The department says they sometimes enter houses and other buildings, where field crickets can chew on clothing. A chirp at night, or hind legs plainly built for jumping, means cricket.
What about giant water bugs and bed bugs?

Neither is a cockroach: giant water bugs are aquatic insects from a different group, and bed bugs are a separate pest. The water bug confusion starts with the word: Texas A&M AgriLife Extension lists waterbug as a nickname for the American cockroach, so water bug can mean two unrelated insects. [A side-by-side comparison of water bugs and cockroaches](/blog/water-bugs-vs-cockroaches) separates the true water bug from the roach that gets called one.

Bed bugs have their own identification guides. A small, flat, brown insect found near a bed is worth checking against [what bed bugs look like](/blog/what-do-bed-bugs-look-like) and [the list of insects that resemble bed bugs](/blog/bugs-that-look-like-bed-bugs) before you assume it is a young roach.
What should you do once you know what it is?
A true pest cockroach is the one that calls for a control program; for the look-alikes, the sources point to leaving them alone or keeping them out.

items: **Wood cockroach.** Penn State Extension recommends exclusion instead of spraying: bring in only as much firewood as you will burn in a few hours, move firewood and debris piles away from the building, caulk cracks in the foundation and around doors and windows, and turn off lights at night so they do not attract flying males.
**Ground beetle.** The Missouri Department of Conservation describes ground beetles as predators of crop-damaging caterpillars and grubs, which is a reason to move one outside instead of killing it.

**Earwig.** UC IPM's advice for earwigs indoors is to sweep or vacuum them up and seal the cracks and entry points they used. It does not recommend insecticide treatments indoors, which it says do little to prevent invasions.

**May beetle or cricket.** The Missouri Department of Conservation says May beetles cannot hurt people. It notes that crickets sometimes enter houses and that field crickets can chew on clothing there, which is a reason to catch one and put it back outside.

**Palmetto bug, or any roach you cannot rule out.** Treat it as a pest cockroach. If it is small and light brown with two dark stripes on the plate behind its head, it fits Texas A&M's description of the German cockroach at 1/2 to 5/8 inch, and [the German cockroach guide](/blog/german-cockroaches) covers identification and the control program for that species.

body.text: For any cockroach that is staying, [a bait-first plan for clearing cockroaches](/blog/how-to-get-rid-of-cockroaches-canada) walks through the steps. If you are still not sure what you have, a sticky trap can hold a specimen to compare against the table above: Texas A&M describes sticky cards as trapping cockroaches and other crawling insects and as most useful for monitoring. A separate guide explains why [glue boards and bait stations do different jobs](/blog/best-roach-traps-canada).

body.title: Save the specimen
body.text: Put the insect in a sealed jar, photograph it beside a ruler marked in inches, and note where and when you found it. Your state's cooperative extension office or a pest professional can use those details to help identify it.

faqs.question: What looks like a cockroach but flies?
faqs.answer: Several insects do. Penn State Extension says male wood cockroaches can fly and are sometimes drawn to lights at night in rural areas. The Missouri Department of Conservation says many ground beetles can fly and are attracted to lights at night, and that May beetles fly clumsily around porch lights. Texas A&M AgriLife Extension says both male and female American cockroaches can fly, so a large flying insect can still be a true cockroach. Check the antennae and the back before deciding.

faqs.question: What is the shiny black beetle that looks like a cockroach?
faqs.answer: It is most likely a ground beetle. The Missouri Department of Conservation describes ground beetles as usually black or brown and often shiny, with hard wing covers that meet in a straight line and often lengthwise grooves. Most are 1/4 to 3/4 inch long. Many hide in dark places by day and come out at night. They prey on caterpillars and grubs, and some species release a foul or irritating chemical when threatened.

faqs.question: Is a palmetto bug a cockroach?
faqs.answer: Yes. Palmetto bug is a nickname, not a separate kind of insect. Texas A&M AgriLife Extension lists waterbug and palmetto bug as other names for the American cockroach, which is reddish brown and 1 1/2 to 2 inches long, with tan to light yellow bands outlining the plate behind its head. Both males and females can fly. A palmetto bug in the house is a true pest cockroach, not a harmless look-alike.

faqs.question: Does finding one wood cockroach mean I have an infestation?
faqs.answer: No. Penn State Extension says wood cockroaches that come indoors die within a few days from dehydration and do not feed or reproduce inside, so one indoors does not point to a breeding population. They get in through foundation cracks, around windows and doors, on firewood, or after being drawn to porch lights. Penn State recommends keeping them out by bringing in only as much firewood as will be burned in a few hours, moving debris piles away from the building, caulking cracks and turning off lights at night, and says pesticides are not necessary or recommended.

faqs.question: Are earwigs dangerous?
faqs.answer: Not to people, according to the University of California Statewide IPM Program. It says earwigs are not harmful and generally do not attack humans, although they can bite if trapped in clothing or sat upon. Large accumulations of earwigs are annoying rather than a health hazard. If a bite swells, keeps getting worse or comes with other symptoms such as trouble breathing, contact a healthcare provider.

faqs.question: Why do these bugs turn up indoors at night?
faqs.answer: Lights and weather explain much of it. The Missouri Department of Conservation says many ground beetles and May beetles are attracted to lights at night, and Penn State Extension says male wood cockroaches can be too. UC IPM says earwigs may come indoors when conditions outside are too dry, too hot or too cold, and the Missouri Department of Conservation says crickets sometimes enter houses and other buildings.
